series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/3] mm/swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the insertion of a new folio into the LRU (Least Recently Used) list out of the swap cache allocator. The previous behavior added the folio to the LRU immediately, but this change defers the insertion until the caller is ready to act on the folio. This is necessary for two upcoming patches: one that moves refault evaluation out of the swap cache allocation and another that implements zswap writeback dropbehind. The functional changes are minimal, as each caller will add the folio to the LRU after allocation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/3] mm/swap: refault on swap-in, not in the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the evaluation of page refaults from the swap cache allocator to the two callers of swap-in functions, which read the slot's shadow before allocation overwrites it. This change prevents inflated workingset_refault_anon and workingset_activate_anon counts due to continuous writeback on certain workloads. The refault is still evaluated before adding the folio to the LRU list, ensuring that PG_workingset/PG_active flags are set correctly.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/3] mm/zswap: preserve the workingset shadow across writeback
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue in the zswap compression algorithm where the workingset shadow is lost during writeback, leading to inaccurate anon refault/workingset accounting. To fix this, the patch preserves the workingset shadow within zswap by parking it in the zswap tree at writeback time, ensuring it outlives the writeback buffer folio. The parked shadow is then handled when the buffer meets one of three fates: swap-in, reclaim, or slot free. This approach ensures accurate accounting for written-back data and fixes a bug introduced by commit aae466b0052e.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series fixes a problem in the zswap writeback path where workingset refaults were being over-counted or lost due to the way swap entries are handled. The patches preserve the eviction cookie (shadow) within zswap, allowing accurate refault detection and reducing the number of refaults by 48-59%. This is achieved without introducing new state in the swap table or slots. The changes also move the refault evaluation out of the swap-cache allocator into the swap-in callers to prevent miscounting writeback allocations as refaults.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/3] mm: swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the insertion of a folio into the LRU (Least Recently Used) list out of the swap cache allocator, allowing callers to decide when to add it to the LRU or free it directly. This change is necessary for zswap writeback, which requires a swap cache folio that can be freed immediately after writeback completes. The patch updates several functions in mm/swap_state.c and mm/zswap.c to reflect this change.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/3] mm: swap: drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's memory management to drop swap cache folios from their cache after writeback completion, rather than leaving them for reclaim later. This is done by extending the existing file dropbehind paths to swap cache folios and setting a flag to indicate that the write has completed. The patch also includes changes to various kernel files to support this new behavior. The goal of this change is to improve memory management efficiency by reducing unnecessary reclaim operations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/3] mm: zswap: drop cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a performance issue in the zswap writeback mechanism by dropping cold folios from the swap cache after writeback completes, reducing unnecessary reclaim scans and keeping cold memory resident for shorter periods.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 1/4] btrfs: split btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() into prealloc and commit phases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() function into three separate functions: prealloc, commit, and free. The prealloc phase allocates memory for a delayed node and item, populates the item data, and inserts it into an rb-tree. The commit phase reserves metadata space and performs the actual insertion. If the allocation fails, the free helper is called to release the allocated resources. This refactoring allows callers to handle ENOMEM errors before modifying on-disk state.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 2/4] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index before btree modification
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to pre-allocate delayed directory index space before modifying the btree. This change prevents ENOMEM failures from leaving the btree in a partially-modified state, which could only be resolved by aborting the transaction. The patch also introduces an optional parameter for callers to provide their own pre-allocated space, and removes a wrapper function that was no longer needed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 3/4] btrfs: handle ENOMEM from btrfs_insert_dir_item() without aborting
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to handle ENOMEM errors when inserting directory items without aborting the transaction. It adds -ENOMEM to the list of recoverable errors in btrfs_add_link() and updates btrfs_create_new_inode() to orphan newly-created inodes instead of aborting on ENOMEM. This change allows create(), mkdir(), mknod(), symlink(), and link() operations to return a graceful -ENOMEM error under memory pressure, preventing filesystem-killing aborts.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 4/4] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index for non-overwrite rename
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to the Btrfs file system that allows it to pre-allocate delayed directory index resources before making any btree modifications during a rename operation. This is done by introducing a new function, `btrfs_prealloc_delayed_dir_index`, which is called in the non-overwrite case of the `btrfs_rename` function. The patch also adds a new parameter to the `btrfs_add_link` function that allows callers to pass pre-allocated delayed directory index resources. This change aims to prevent ENOMEM errors from occurring after btree state has changed, by returning -ENOMEM early if the pre-allocation fails.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a long-standing issue in Btrfs where memory allocation failures can cause the file system to abort during synchronous directory operations. The patches rework the code to perform allocations upfront, before reaching the point of potential abortion. This approach is designed to work in conjunction with another patch series that introduces GFP_NOFAIL memory allocation behavior. Although this series does not cover all possible cases where ENOMEM errors can occur, it aims to mitigate a relatively rare but significant problem dating back to at least 2011.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 04/57] mm/collapse: rename mthp_present_ptes to eligible_ptes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the 'mthp_present_ptes' bitmap to 'eligible_ptes' in the Linux kernel's memory management (mm) module. The rename is motivated by the fact that a bit being set in this bitmap does not necessarily mean the page is present, but rather that it has passed certain checks during a scan. The patch makes no functional changes and only updates the naming of the bitmap to better reflect its meaning.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 05/57] mm/collapse: state what a collapse may do in the policy
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new struct collapse_policy to store the policy decisions made by the caller of the collapse code. The policy is filled in once per scan pass by khugepaged and once per call by MADV_COLLAPSE. This change simplifies the collapse code by removing the need for it to look up who called it, and instead allows it to read from the stored policy. The patch also removes a NULL check in collapse_file() as it is no longer necessary.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 06/57] mm/collapse: move the smallest collapse order to collapse.h
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the definition of the smallest collapse order from khugepaged.c to a shared header file, collapse.h. This is done because the smallest collapse order is a property of collapse, not just khugepaged. The change prepares for the collapse engine, which will size its per-window arrays based on this floor. No functional changes are intended by this patch.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 07/57] mm/collapse: sketch the new anonymous collapse engine
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new anonymous collapse engine to improve the scalability and functionality of memory collapsing in Linux. The current implementation is limited by its exclusive lock, which stops every fault in the address space for each huge page. The new engine addresses this issue by quiescing its sources like migration does, allowing it to run under mmap_read throughout. It also carries a batch of windows through each step together and makes decisions per window rather than per table. This patch lays out the design of the new engine without filling in the implementation details yet.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 08/57] mm/collapse: scan a table for what a collapse could use
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a function to scan a page table and identify potential candidates for collapsing, which is a process of merging multiple pages into one. The function sets bits in the cc->eligible_ptes bitmap for every present, anonymous, non-UFFD-armed PTE that is on the LRU and unlocked. This advice is then used by the freeze to settle any questions about the collapse candidates. The patch also handles cases where a partial table is scanned and ensures that limits are applied per PMD, rather than globally.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 09/57] mm/collapse: collect candidate windows into a round
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a feature to collect candidate windows into rounds, which are batches of memory that can be collapsed together. The size of each round is capped at 32MB due to memory allocation and fault latency considerations. A dense table is collapsed as multiple rounds rather than one. The patch introduces new macros to define the maximum number of candidates per round and the batch size. It also updates the collapse_anon_pmd function to collect candidates into a round until it's full or selection is complete, then run the round and repeat the process.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 10/57] mm/collapse: run a round and feed the outcomes back
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new function, collapse_round(), which runs a round of candidate evaluation and classification. The function iterates over the batch of candidates, applying passes to each one until it reaches a freeze point or the table is abandoned. The outcomes of these evaluations are then fed back into selection through the collapse_classify_result() function, allowing for decisions on what comes next in the process.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 11/57] mm/collapse: sketch the passes of a round
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new concept called 'rounds' in the collapse mechanism, which is a sequence of passes over the same batch. A round consists of three parts: before any lock, under mmap_read, and from freeze onwards. The patch lays out this sequence with stub passes for each part, including a fault-in pass that may have to sleep and drop the lock. If a fault has to wait, it is reported as SCAN_LOCK_DROPPED and the round takes the lock again and runs the pass afresh a bounded number of times.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 12/57] mm/collapse: allocate a destination per candidate
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allocates a destination per candidate in the collapse mechanism. The destination is a folio of the candidate's order, charged to the memcg, and is used when the system is frozen. The allocation process involves two main functions: `collapse_alloc` and `collapse_provision`. `collapse_alloc` handles the allocation for one candidate with the given GFP flags, while `collapse_provision` is responsible for requesting allocations from the collapse mechanism without direct reclaim. The patch also introduces a new function called `collapse_deposit`, which secures page table allocations ahead of freezing. Overall, this patch aims to improve the efficiency and reliability of the collapse mechanism by providing a dedicated destination for each candidate.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary: Lance Yang noted that folio_memcg_alloc_deferred() passes GFP_KERNEL to the deferred_split_lru allocation, which includes __GFP_DIRECT_RECLAIM, potentially bypassing the direct reclaim stripping in collapse_provision(). He suggested modifying folio_memcg_alloc_deferred() to use the gfp with direct reclaim stripped.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author acknowledged that passing down GFP flags is necessary and agreed to make the change.
review_comments.raw_body:
Right. Passing down gfp is the right thing to do here.

Thanks, will fix.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 13/57] mm/collapse: revalidate a round against the VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch revalidates a round against the VMA (memory area) in the Linux kernel's memory management system. It checks that the mm is not exiting and has not had THP (Transparent Huge Pages) disabled, and that the VMA still allows every provisioned candidate. The patch also finds the PTE table again to ensure it hasn't changed since the scan and allocation dropped the mmap_lock. If a VMA shrank or was replaced by a smaller one, candidates that no longer fit within its window are dropped. Finally, the patch settles the batch's span for the invalidate operation.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 14/57] mm/collapse: fault the sources in before the freeze
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the collapse functionality in the Linux kernel to fault in pages before freezing them. It ensures that each candidate slot is either a hole, the zero page, or an exclusively owned present page. The patch walks through each candidate slot and lets the fault path handle any necessary actions, such as unsharing pages shared with fork children or reading back swap entries. If a page cannot be faulted in after multiple attempts, it is left to the freeze function to refuse it. The patch also introduces a new retry mechanism for swap-in faults below the PMD order and reports dropped locks accordingly.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 15/57] mm/collapse: check what a candidate would freeze
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new function to check whether a candidate can be frozen in the mm/collapse module. The function walks through every slot covered by the candidate, under the table's ptl, and checks if all conditions are met for freezing. These conditions include that the folio is anonymous, not uffd-armed, and has no live mappings outside of the current span. The patch also adds a new trace event to track the scan result. If the candidate passes these checks, it can be frozen, otherwise the round only incurs the cost of the walk.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 16/57] mm/collapse: freeze the sources behind migration entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch freezes the sources behind migration entries in the Linux kernel's memory management system, ensuring that faults and GUP-slow operations wait on a folio lock before accessing the source. The freeze is implemented using two barriers to maintain reachability order, preventing writeback from bypassing the freeze. A ranged TLB flush is used to ensure all frozen sources are updated before releasing the ptl lock. The patch also includes a mechanism for restoring displaced values in case of failure.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer noted that deferred_split_isolate() can remove a source folio from deferred_split_lru while its refcount is frozen by collapse_freeze_candidate(), which causes folio_try_get() to fail, and requested the lock be dropped before calling try_to_unmap().

The reviewer noted that collapse_unfreeze_candidate() does not add the source folio back to the deferred split queue after restoring it, potentially leaving underused or partially mapped folios off the queue.

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern that the premise in deferred_split_isolate() is false: !folio_try_get() doesn't mean lost race with folio_put(). They proposed a fix to return LRU_SKIP if the folio try get fails, and asked Johannes for clarification on their suggestion.

review_comments.author: Johannes Weiner
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer questioned whether 'freeze' means exclusive or non-exclusive locking, and asked who would clean up the partially_mapped state

The reviewer suggested modifying the behavior of folio_put() to leave the item on the LRU when there is a race with the refcount going zero, allowing the other side to deal with/clean up the partially_mapped state as appropriate.
review_comments.raw_body:
I suppose you mean, not exclusively. But it can also mean that. And
then the question is, who cleans up the partially_mapped state.

---

Ah. The idea being: leave the item on the LRU when there is a race
with the refcount going zero; and then it's up to that other side to
deal with/clean up the partially_mapped state as appropriate. Thus:

folio_put()
  __folio_put()
    folio_unqueue_deferred_split()
      if __list_lru_del():
        // clear partially_mapped state & stats

will always succeed, even if it races with the shrinker. And you are
also guaranteed on the collapse side that the state won't vanish from
underneath you.

I think that should work. Usama?

review_comments.author: Usama Arif
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Usama Arif noted that if the reference to a folio is not obtained, the owner of the reference should decide how partially_mapped is treated for that folio, and suggested that clearing partially_mapped in folio_ref_freeze() is incorrect
review_comments.raw_body:
Kiryl's suggestion makes sense. I think there is a bug here. If we dont
get the reference, whoever owns the reference should decide how partially_mapped
is treated for that folio:

- If its the last folio_put(), it will clear partially_mapped and cleanup
after itself.
- If its folio_ref_freeze(), clearing partially_mapped is wrong (which we
are currently doing in deferred_split_isolate)

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary: Lance Yang noted that patch 16 introduces a state-loss bug when collapse rolls back a partially mapped folio because deferred_split_isolate() can dequeue the folio and clear its PG_partially_mapped flag before freeze is rolled back, leaving it in an inconsistent state. He suggested using LRU_SKIP instead of returning LRU_REMOVED to avoid this issue.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 17/57] mm/collapse: copy the sources into the destinations
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, collapse_copy, which copies pages from source candidates to their corresponding destinations in memory. The copy operation is performed for each candidate that has both frozen and has a destination folio. If the source page does not exist, it is zero-filled. The function also handles machine checks on source pages and records any failures. The patch modifies the collapse_provision function to publish each destination folio in place of its corresponding sources.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 18/57] mm/collapse: install the destinations at PTE level
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds functionality to install the destinations at PTE level in the mm/collapse code. It includes a verify step to ensure that the window is still the round's to publish, and an abort step to undo a frozen candidate that cannot be published. The patch also handles publishing, which involves updating the destination's rmap and LRU insertion before its PTEs are updated. Additionally, it adds a terminal layer for PMD-order candidates and includes code to handle zapped slots and racing MADV_DONTNEED operations.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary: Lance Yang noted that KSM zero-page accounting gets out of sync when a saved zero PTE is restored in the collapse_abort_candidate() function, as it does not drop the counters if the PTE was previously marked dirty by ksm_map_zero_page(). He suggested adding a new function collapse_unmap_zero_pages() to handle this case and proposed modifying the collapse_install_pmd() and collapse_install() functions to call this new function.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 19/57] mm/collapse: install a PMD leaf as the terminal layer
series_items.patch_summary: This patch installs a PMD (Page Map Directory) leaf as the terminal layer in the mm/collapse code. It does this by verifying, detaching, and then depositing a fresh PMD table under the pmd lock, ensuring that no pmd_none() window exists during the operation. This approach allows PMD collapse to run under mmap_read like other operations, and it handles potential racing conditions and aborts. The patch also ensures that the detached table is not quiesced immediately, but rather held until walkers finish with it, resulting in a one-time cost of a transient table page per PMD collapse.

review_comments.author: Lance Yang
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Lance Yang noted that the patch does not handle the PAE case correctly and referenced a specific commit (146b42e07494) where pmdp_get_lockless_sync() was added for this purpose, requesting that the patch be updated to include this functionality.

Reviewer Lance Yang noted that the current implementation of collapse_install_pmd() does not include pmdp_get_lockless_sync() between pmdp_collapse_flush() and map_anon_folio_pmd_nopf(), which can cause split-PMD readers to observe unmatched halves across the transition from old PMD to new leaf PMD. Lance suggested adding pmdp_get_lockless_sync() right after pmdp_collapse_flush() to prevent this issue.

review_comments.author: Jann Horn
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Jann Horn questioned the atomicity of PMD table updates, pointing out that pmdp_collapse_flush() clears the PMD entry while holding the PMD table spinlock, but codepaths like zap_pmd_range() may not take this lock and can thus race with MADV_DONTNEED or zap_vma_range(), potentially making the zap ineffective.

Reviewer Jann Horn noted that the patch's claim of no pmd_none() window existing is incorrect because concurrent rmap-walks into the PMD can occur, potentially looking at stale PTEs.

The reviewer questioned whether the old table contains migration entries at the point when its spinlock is dropped and it's scheduled for freeing, suggesting that zeroing all PTEs in the old table before dropping its lock could prevent a concurrent pte_offset_map_rw_nolock() from seeing dangling migration entries.
review_comments.raw_body:
What do you mean by "atomic" and "no pmd_none() window ever exists"?
Is that supposed to be with respect to a subset of readers?

While the PMD table spinlock is held, you clear the PMD entry
(pmdp_collapse_flush) and set it to a new value
(map_anon_folio_pmd_nopf). But codepaths that walk page tables don't
take that spinlock unless they already know they're in a THP case.

zap_pmd_range() does not lock the PMD table before checking
pmd_none(), and if that is true, it skips over the PMD. I think this
means that THP collapse can race with MADV_DONTNEED or zap_vma_range()
such that the zap wrongly has no effect?

---

To be clear, we can concurrently rmap-walk into the PMD, right?
Because we might be looking at a different folio which was created in
the parent process or something like that? And so a
page_vma_mapped_walk() without PVMW_SYNC might look at stale PTEs?
(Which may or may not be fine, but would not be what this commit
message claims.)

---

What does old_table contain at this point - migration entries? I
wonder if we should zero all the PTEs inside it before dropping its
spinlock and scheduling its freeing, so that a concurrent
pte_offset_map_rw_nolock()+spin_lock() wouldn't see dangling migration
entries. (I'm not sure if we actually have a codepath that does that,
but even if not, this seems like it might cause problems later.)

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 20/57] mm/collapse: put the sources back
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called `collapse_putback` which is responsible for putting back sources that were previously frozen during the collapse process. It iterates over each installed candidate, lowers the barriers raised by the freeze, and wakes up faulters that were sleeping on source folios' locks. The order of operations within a span is crucial: unfreeze first, then drop the rmap, unlock, and finally drop references strictly last. This patch also removes stale swapcache entries as the copy has replaced what it described.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 21/57] mm/collapse: settle whatever the round reached
series_items.patch_summary: This patch completes the last pass of a round in the collapse function, handling candidates that never froze and releasing resources held by refused candidates. It records the result for candidates that were selected but not frozen, and releases folios and tables allocated to candidates that were not installed. The patch also updates the count of installed candidates and returns this value.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 22/57] mm/collapse: walk a table with a selection cursor
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new feature to walk a table with a selection cursor, which is used to select candidate windows from the table. The cursor advances at emission and never rewinds, and it assumes that every attempt will succeed within a round. The patch also keeps track of non-present PTEs accepted by the scan in cc->scan_unmapped, adding them back only for PMD candidates. The selection process is bounded by huge page alignment and the largest enabled order.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 23/57] mm/collapse: give a refused region a second chance
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a mechanism to give refused regions in the Linux kernel's memory management system a second chance by storing them in a stack and re-probing them at a lower order. The classification of regions is based on their outcome, which can be one of four: collapse, allocation failure, refusal due to smaller window, or refusal due to in-window allocation miss. The patch also updates the `collapse_anon_pmd` function to report the outcomes of each table in order of precedence.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 24/57] mm/collapse: report each candidate's outcome to tracing
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new tracepoint to the Linux kernel's tracing system, allowing the outcome of each candidate in the memory collapse process to be reported. The tracepoint provides information about the window address and order, the pass that made the decision, and the result of that decision. This allows for better understanding and debugging of the memory collapse process.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 25/57] mm/collapse: collapse anonymous memory with the new engine
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new engine to collapse anonymous memory in the Linux kernel. The old mechanism is replaced, and the new one allows collapsing of anonymous memory under mmap_read lock instead of holding mmap_write for its duration. This change improves performance by allowing faults elsewhere in the address space to continue while the collapse operation runs. Additionally, even if a table cannot be collapsed into a single huge page, the engine still identifies the largest windows within it. The patch updates several files including mm/collapse.c and mm/khugepaged.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 26/57] mm/collapse: give collapse_single_pmd() the range to work on
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the collapse_single_pmd() function to accept a range instead of deriving it from its start point. The function is updated to pass the end of the range as an argument to both the scan and collapse operations, which already support partial tables. This change prepares for scanning VMAs that span less than a whole table and does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 27/57] mm/collapse: scan the windows a VMA can hold
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged algorithm to scan VMAs in a more efficient way by considering the largest order of windows that a VMA can hold, rather than only scanning PMD-aligned addresses. This change allows khugepaged to reach and collapse larger VMAs, including those with smaller THP orders enabled. The patch also removes unnecessary assertions and clamping logic.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 28/57] mm/collapse: remove the mechanism the engine replaces
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the mechanism that the new engine replaces in the mm/collapse code. The old anonymous collapse functionality is no longer needed as its entry point was rewired to the new engine, and all functions below it lost their last caller. The patch deletes a chain of functions including scan, mTHP order walk, collapse itself, isolation, swap-in, copy with success and failure paths, PTE release helpers, folio_pte_referenced(), and pmd-still-valid check. However, some functions like alloc_charge_folio() and hugepage_vma_revalidate() are left intact as they are still called by file paths and MADV_COLLAPSE. Four tracepoints also lose their only emitter but their definitions remain in the code.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 29/57] mm/collapse: move what a collapse is judged on into collapse.c
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves various functions and data from khugepaged.c to collapse.c, making the latter self-sufficient and reducing its dependency on the former. The moved functions include checks for PMD state, order calculations, and NUMA heuristics. This change aims to make the code more modular and easier to maintain.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 30/57] mm/collapse: name the max_ptes ceiling after collapse
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames a constant in the Linux kernel's memory management code to better reflect its purpose. The constant, previously named KHUGEPAGED_MAX_PTES_LIMIT, is used as a ceiling for the maximum number of page table entries (PTEs) that can be collapsed by the khugepaged process. It has been renamed to COLLAPSE_MAX_PTES_LIMIT to match other constants in the same header file and to improve clarity. The change affects several files in the kernel's memory management code, including collapse.c, collapse.h, and khugepaged.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 31/57] mm/khugepaged: count collapses where khugepaged makes them
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged code to count page collapses within its own walk, rather than relying on the caller to update a shared counter. This simplifies the code and eliminates unnecessary checks for whether the collapse is being performed by the khugepaged daemon or not. The change prepares the way for moving the dispatcher into a separate file from where it can access static variables in khugepaged.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 32/57] mm/collapse: move the file collapse into collapse.c
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the file collapse mechanism from khugepaged.c to collapse.c, where it will be part of a unified collapse engine. The move includes functions related to file collapse, PTE-mapped THP recollapse, and table retraction. Five helpers are made static as they no longer have external callers. The patch is a pure motion of code with minimal changes, resulting in the removal of 1075 lines from khugepaged.c and addition of 1090 lines to collapse.c.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 33/57] mm/collapse: split collapse into a scan and a run
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the collapse functionality into two separate functions: collapse_scan_pmd() and collapse_run_pmd(). The scan function checks if a table needs to be collapsed, while the run function performs the actual collapse operation. This change improves lock management and reduces unnecessary lock acquisitions, making the code more efficient and easier to understand.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 34/57] mm/collapse: implement MADV_COLLAPSE in madvise.c
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the implementation of MADV_COLLAPSE from khugepaged.c to madvise.c, where it belongs among other madvise operations. The move simplifies the code and removes unnecessary dependencies between the daemon's file and the syscall implementation. The patch also updates the declaration in huge_mm.h and adjusts the eligibility test for collapse. The changes do not affect the functionality of MADV_COLLAPSE itself.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 35/57] mm/madvise: drop MADV_COLLAPSE's redundant mm reference
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes an unnecessary mmgrab() reference in the madvise_collapse() function, which holds a reference to the memory management structure (mm_struct) across its work. The reference was redundant because other parts of the code already hold references to the address space and task's memory, ensuring it remains alive during the operation.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 36/57] mm/collapse: report what the scan found
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new trace event called mm_collapse_scan to report the results of an anonymous memory scan in the Linux kernel. The scan reports information such as the address scanned, the number of holes or zero-page slots, the number of swapped-out pages, and the orders that survived the scan. This information is used to determine whether a table should be refused outright or if it can still try certain orders. The patch also adds a new function called trace_mm_collapse_scan to report this information through tracing. This patch is part of a larger series of patches (36/57) and aims to improve the reporting and debugging capabilities of the kernel's memory management system.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 37/57] mm/collapse: report what the fault-in pass paid
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds reporting of faults taken during the fault-in pass in the Linux kernel's memory collapse functionality. The fault-in pass is responsible for handling swap reads and CoW breaks, but its performance was previously invisible. This patch introduces a new trace event called mm_collapse_faultin that captures the number of faults taken and their outcome. This information will help identify slow collapses or khugepaged workloads. The reporting occurs before the walk and after the mmap_lock is dropped on failure to ensure safety.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 38/57] mm/collapse: report the round, and what it made faulters wait
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new event, mm_collapse_round, to report the time it takes for a thread to wait on a source due to batching. The event includes information about the number of candidates collected and installed, as well as the outcome of the collapse operation. This is intended to help evaluate whether larger batches are beneficial by measuring the wait time for faulters. The patch introduces a new field in the trace events and updates the collapse_finish function to return the number of candidates installed.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 39/57] mm/collapse: name the file collapse's tracepoints after collapse
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames two tracepoints in the Linux kernel to reflect their association with the collapse mechanism, rather than khugepaged. The renamed tracepoints are mm_collapse_scan_file and mm_collapse_file, which were previously named mm_khugepaged_scan_file and mm_khugepaged_collapse_file respectively. This change is necessary because the collapse mechanism now uses the same entry points as khugepaged, and the old names could cause issues with BPF programs that rely on these tracepoints.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 40/57] mm/collapse: remove the tracepoints of the mechanism that is gone
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes four tracepoints that were no longer needed after the anonymous memory mechanism was deleted. The removed tracepoints are mm_khugepaged_scan_pmd, mm_collapse_huge_page, mm_collapse_huge_page_isolate, and mm_collapse_huge_page_swapin. These tracepoints had lost their only emitter and were no longer useful. The patch also removes two entries from the raw_tp_null_args[] array that could never match again. The engine's own events now cover the same ground as these removed tracepoints.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 41/57] mm/collapse: give collapse its own trace header
series_items.patch_summary: This patch renames the trace header from huge_memory.h to collapse.h, matching the new name of the kernel module that builds the tracepoints. The rename is done to better reflect the purpose and origin of the events in this header. Additionally, the enum collapse_pass is moved out of mm/collapse.h into collapse.c where the tracepoints are built. This change also updates khugepaged's selftest and other references to the old name.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 42/57] mm/collapse: allow error injection into the freeze
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows error injection into a specific function, collapse_freeze_candidate(), which is responsible for freezing memory regions during the collapse process. The goal is to test and exercise scenarios where a candidate is refused due to certain conditions, such as a co-mapper appearing between sweeps or GUP-fast pinning. The patch introduces error injection using the ALLOW_ERROR_INJECTION macro, allowing developers to simulate these refusal scenarios intentionally.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 43/57] mm/khugepaged: check the scan budget before the work, not after
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged code to check the scan budget before performing work, rather than after. This ensures that a pass over an address space of thousands of VMAs does not exceed the allocated budget. The changes involve adding checks for the budget at the top of both loops in the collapse_scan_mm_slot function and advancing the khugepaged_scan.address pointer when skipping a VMA to prevent walking from the same place every pass.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 44/57] mm/khugepaged: hold the address space open across a scan
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged code to hold a reference to the address space's mm_users count instead of relying on the barrier in __khugepaged_exit() and taking mmap_lock for writing. This change allows khugepaged to operate under a per-VMA lock, which does not hold mmap_lock, without causing exit_mmap() to free page tables prematurely. The patch also introduces new functions to check if an address space's owner has gone or if it is disabled from THP completely.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 45/57] mm/collapse: take a per-VMA read lock for the round
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the collapse functionality to take a per-VMA read lock instead of holding the mmap_lock across multiple operations. This change allows writers in other parts of the mm to proceed without waiting for the collapse operation, which can be lengthy. The patch also introduces a new error code SCAN_VMA_LOCK to handle cases where the VMA is being written to and cannot be locked for reading. The collapse_revalidate function now checks if the VMA still covers the collected range after the lock has been taken.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 46/57] mm/khugepaged: scan under a per-VMA read lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged functionality to take a per-VMA read lock instead of holding the mmap_lock for the whole address space walk. This change allows multiple scans to run concurrently, improving performance. The patch also updates the cursor movement and error handling mechanisms to accommodate the new locking scheme.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 47/57] mm/madvise: collapse under a per-VMA read lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the MADV_COLLAPSE functionality in the Linux kernel to use a per-VMA read lock instead of acquiring and releasing the mmap_lock. This change allows multiple writers to access the address space simultaneously, reducing contention and improving performance. The patch also introduces new error handling for cases where the VMA cannot be locked or is being written to. Remote madvise operations are exempt from this change due to their unique requirements.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 48/57] mm/collapse: assert the mm reference the engine relies on
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the collapse engine in the Linux kernel to assert that a reference to the mm_struct exists before performing certain operations. The patch addresses a bug where the engine was checking if the mm_users count had reached zero, which is not possible due to the way callers hold references on mm_users. Instead, it checks if collapsing has been disabled by prctl and asserts that a reference exists in other cases. This change ensures that a caller with no reference on mm_users will be detected as an error in debug builds.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 49/57] mm/khugepaged: drop the mmap_lock barrier from __khugepaged_exit()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes a redundant barrier in the __khugepaged_exit() function, which was previously taking the mmap_lock for writing and dropping it to wait for a scan holding it for reading before destroying page tables. However, since the scan now holds a reference on mm_users until its completion, it cannot be in flight at this point, making the barrier unnecessary.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 50/57] selftests/mm: attribute collapses by candidate event alone
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the selftests/mm module to count collapses of a window by matching candidate events instead of isolate events. The recorded PFNs are no longer needed, so they have been removed from the array. This change is part of a larger series of patches and is intended to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the test.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 51/57] selftests/mm: cover collapse inside a sub-PMD VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two new test cases to the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c file, which cover the collapse of memory inside a sub-page map directory (PMD) VMA. The first case tests collapsing an mTHP in a VMA that holds exactly one window, while the second case tests collapsing multiple windows within a single VMA. This patch addresses a limitation in the old mechanism, where VMAs smaller than a PMD were not considered valid collapse targets, resulting in missed opportunities for memory compaction on systems with large page sizes.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 52/57] selftests/mm: cover a hole-y window in a sub-PMD VMA
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test case to the selftests/mm suite to cover a previously untested scenario where a partially populated window in a sub-PMU VMA is collapsed. The test checks that unfaulted slots are zero-filled and faulted pages remain unchanged after collapse. The test uses the khugepaged tool to simulate the collapse operation and verify its correctness.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 53/57] selftests/mm: cover collapse of mlocked ranges
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds self-tests to cover the collapse of mlocked ranges in the Linux kernel. The tests ensure that when an mlocked range is collapsed, the source pages are properly munlocked and the new folio arrives locked as expected. The tests also verify that the collapse process works correctly under contention between threads locking and unlocking random spans across a region. The patch introduces a new function `collapse_order_mlocked` to handle this specific case of collapsing mlocked ranges.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 54/57] selftests/mm: cover collapse beside a MADV_FREE'd page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the khugepaged selftest to handle a situation where one page in a PMD is marked as MADV_FREE'd, preventing the entire table from being collapsed by khugepaged. The test creates a lazyfree page and checks that the surrounding windows collapse correctly while leaving the lazyfree page intact. This ensures that reclaim can still drop the page's contents without affecting other pages in the same PMD.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 55/57] selftests/mm: cover collapse beside a pinned page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a test to the selftests/mm/khugepaged module to cover the case where khugepaged collapses memory beside a pinned page. The test pin one page using gup_test and then checks that the rest of the table is collapsed, the window holding the pinned page is not collapsed, and the pinned page remains backed by an order-0 folio. If any of these conditions are not met, the test fails. The patch also skips the test if CONFIG_GUP_TEST or root privileges are not available.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 56/57] selftests/mm: cover the scaled max_ptes_shared limit
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test case to the selftests/mm/khugepaged.c file, which covers the scaled max_ptes_shared limit. The current implementation of max_ptes_shared counts PTEs in whole PMDs but fails to account for smaller ranges that are scanned in full and judged against the same setting. This leads to incorrect results when checking if a range should collapse. To fix this issue, the patch introduces a new test case that checks both directions in one sub-PMD range with a forked child holding shared sources. The counts used in the test come from the current max_ptes_shared rather than being hardcoded, allowing the test to follow the setting and order it runs at.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 57/57] MAINTAINERS: add an entry for collapse
series_items.patch_summary: This RFC patch proposes to separate the THP collapse logic into its own body of code, mm/collapse.c, and add a new section for it in the MAINTAINERS file. The existing THP entry would be updated accordingly.

review_comments.raw_body:
From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

Anonymous collapse is held back in two ways that its current shape cannot
be patched out of.

Functionally, an mTHP is collapsed only when the whole PMD-sized window
qualifies: collapse_scan_pmd() reaches mthp_collapse() only on
SCAN_SUCCEED.  One PTE that disqualifies itself -- uffd-armed, not
anonymous, clean lazyfree, off the LRU, pinned -- takes the whole table
with it.  A 2M range with a single such page yields nothing, even where
the half beside it would collapse perfectly well.

For scalability, collapse_huge_page() holds mmap_write across a collapse,
and anon_vma_lock_write() with it, then does the same again for the next
huge page.  Every collapse stops every fault in the address space, one
huge page at a time.

The new engine addresses both.  It quiesces its sources the way migration
does: migration entries in their PTEs, then a frozen refcount.  That is
enough to make the copy safe without the exclusive lock, so the engine
runs under mmap_read throughout.

It also carries a batch of windows through each step together, rather
than one window through all of them.  Its verdict is per window rather
than per table, so a table that cannot become one huge page still yields
the largest windows inside it.

Lay the design out first and fill it in afterwards.  What arrives here is
the shape of the engine: the two entry points, and a comment at the top
of mm/collapse.c mapping the whole call tree.  Every step below them is a
stub, filled in before the anonymous path is pointed at the engine.

collapse_scan_anon_pmd() finds the table, asks the VMA which orders it
allows, scans it, and leaves in the collapse_control what a collapse
could use.  collapse_anon_pmd() takes that range and cuts it into
windows.

The line between the two is where the lock goes.  A scan only reads a VMA
and a page table, so it keeps the mmap_lock it was called under and hands
it back.  A collapse allocates, copies and flushes, so it is called
without the lock and takes it again for each round of its own.  Nothing
then has to tell a caller whether the lock survived a call, and a caller
that finds nothing to collapse never gives the lock up at all.

Nothing calls either entry point yet; the anonymous path keeps using the
mechanism the engine replaces.

+#include "internal.h"

+/*
+ * Anonymous collapse, in rounds.
+ *
+ * The folios mapped across a window of PTEs become one folio of that window's
+ * order, with the sources quiesced by the two barriers migration uses --
+ * migration entries in their PTEs, then a frozen refcount -- so the copy itself
+ * needs no lock.  The engine runs under mmap_read throughout.
+ *
+ * A round carries a batch of candidate windows through the passes together,
+ * rather than carrying one window through the whole collapse.  [ptl] and
+ * [pmd lock] mark a pass that takes that lock and drops it again, so no
+ * page-table lock is ever held across passes; the source folio locks are the
+ * exception, held from freeze to putback.  [rcu] marks a pass that takes no
+ * page-table lock at all and reads the table racily, which only the scan does.
+ *
+ * Allocation happens on both sides of the freeze, and which side comes first
+ * matters.  collapse_provision() tries first, inside the window and after the
+ * freeze, with reclaim masked out of the gfp: the sources are frozen by then,
+ * so a faulter on one of them waits for this allocation.  A candidate the
+ * allocator has nothing ready for is not failed -- it goes back to selection,
+ * and collapse_reserve() allocates for it before the next round freezes
+ * anything, outside the window, where reclaim costs khugepaged its own
+ * progress and nobody else's wait.
+ *
+ * That second chance needs the policy's gfp to allow reclaim at all.  When it
+ * does not, a retry would miss the same way, so the first miss is the answer.
+ *
+ * collapse_scan_anon_pmd()            judge one PTE table's worth of a VMA
+ * `- collapse_scan_table()            [rcu] a bit per PTE a collapse can use
+ *
+ * collapse_anon_pmd()                 cut windows from those bits, run them
+ * |- collapse_next_candidate()        the next window worth attempting
+ * `- collapse_run_batch()             run the batch, then classify it
+ *    |- collapse_round()              below
+ *    `- collapse_classify_result()    carry on / lower / abandon
+ *       `- collapse_push_retry()      queue it for a lower order
+ *
+ * collapse_round()                    one batch of candidates
+ * |- collapse_reserve()               second try for what the last round
+ * |                                   missed, with reclaim; sleeps
+ * |- collapse_deposit()               a page table per PMD-order candidate
+ * |- collapse_revalidate()            check the VMA and the table survived
+ * |- collapse_faultin()               make the sources present and exclusive;
+ * |                                   sleeps, and may leave the lock dropped
+ * |- collapse_freeze()                raise the barriers [ptl], flush the TLB
+ * |- collapse_provision()             first try for every other destination,
+ * |                                   without reclaim: the sources are frozen
+ * |- collapse_copy()                  copy into the destinations; sleeps
+ * |- collapse_install()               publish them [ptl], or [pmd lock] and a
+ * |                                   second TLB flush at the PMD order
+ * |- collapse_putback()               lower the barriers, in order
+ * `- collapse_finish()                settle whatever the round reached
+ *
+ * Every slot of a candidate is a real source, a hole (pte_none, zero-filled
+ * and re-verified still-none at install), or the zeropage (cleared at freeze,
+ * zero-filled).  Sources come in "spans" -- consecutive PTEs mapping
+ * consecutive pages of one folio -- so partially mapped and compound sources
+ * collapse too: any order below the window's is a source, and a PMD candidate
+ * takes even a PTE-mapped THP of its own order.
+ *
+ * Nothing calls any of this yet: the anon path still uses the mechanism it
+ * replaces, and is switched over once both halves are complete.
+ */
+
+/*
+ * Scan the PTEs between @start and @end and record what a collapse could use: a
+ * bit in cc->eligible_ptes for every PTE that may be a source.  Returns
+ * SCAN_SUCCEED when every PTE in the range qualified, otherwise the reason one
+ * did not, and narrows cc->select_orders to what is still worth trying here.
+ */
+static enum scan_result collapse_scan_table(struct vm_area_struct *vma,
+					    pmd_t *pmd, unsigned long start,
+					    unsigned long end,
+					    struct collapse_control *cc)
+{
+	return SCAN_SUCCEED;
+}
+
+/* Everything a table is judged on starts empty for each table */
+static void collapse_anon_scan_init(struct collapse_control *cc)
+{
+	bitmap_zero(cc->eligible_ptes, MAX_PTRS_PER_PTE);
+	memset(cc->node_load, 0, sizeof(cc->node_load));
+	nodes_clear(cc->alloc_nmask);
+
+	cc->select_orders = 0;
+	cc->nr_collapsed = 0;
+}
+
+/*
+ * Judge one table's worth of @vma, leaving in @cc what a collapse could use:
+ * which orders are still worth attempting, and why the table was turned down if
+ * some order was.  Holds mmap_lock throughout -- it only reads -- and a caller
+ * that acts on what it found hands the range to collapse_anon_pmd() afterwards,
+ * without the lock.
+ */
+static enum scan_result __maybe_unused
+collapse_scan_anon_pmd(struct vm_area_struct *vma, unsigned long start,
+		       unsigned long end, struct collapse_control *cc)
+{
+	const unsigned long pmd_addr = start & HPAGE_PMD_MASK;
+	struct mm_struct *mm = vma->vm_mm;
+	pmd_t *pmd;
+
+	/* One table's worth at most, not empty, and inside the VMA */
+	VM_WARN_ON_ONCE(end > pmd_addr + HPAGE_PMD_SIZE || start >= end);
+	VM_WARN_ON_ONCE(start < vma->vm_start || end > vma->vm_end);
+
+	cc->scan_refusal = find_pmd_or_thp_or_none(mm, pmd_addr, &pmd);
+	if (cc->scan_refusal != SCAN_SUCCEED) {
+		cc->progress++;
+		return cc->scan_refusal;
+	}
+
+	/* Cleared only once a table has turned out to be there */
+	collapse_anon_scan_init(cc);
+
+	cc->select_orders = collapse_possible_orders(vma, vma->vm_flags,
+						     cc->policy.tva_type);
+	if (!cc->select_orders) {
+		cc->scan_refusal = SCAN_VMA_CHECK;
+		return cc->scan_refusal;
+	}
+
+	/* The scan narrows select_orders to whatever is left worth trying */
+	cc->scan_refusal = collapse_scan_table(vma, pmd, start, end, cc);
+
+	return cc->scan_refusal;
+}
+
+/*
+ * Cut the table into candidate windows and collapse what fits, from the
+ * largest order downwards.  Returns what the table yielded: a collapse, or
+ * the reason it did not.
+ */
+static enum scan_result __maybe_unused
+collapse_anon_pmd(struct mm_struct *mm, unsigned long start, unsigned long end,
+		  struct collapse_control *cc)
+{
+	return SCAN_FAIL;
+}

IIRC that discussion predates Hugh's pte_offset_map() rework -- since
0d940a9b270b the helper takes rcu_read_lock() and fails if the pmd is
none, !present or huge, so mmap_write is no longer what keeps a pte
walker out.  MADV_DONTNEED is still not excluded, and the engine does not
try to: the install re-reads every slot under the ptl and publishes only
if it still holds the migration entry this round put there, leaving a
zapped slot alone and dropping the rmap the frozen source still held.

--

I read the TODO list and I'll pick from it -- though I notice the
technical debt section includes "Literally all of the code in
mm/huge_memory.c and mm/khugepaged.c", which I'd argue this series is a
fairly committed attempt at :)

One clean up I wanted to do is consolidate code by functionality, not by
the THP/non-THP split.  Move all page fault handler code into mm/fault.c,
unmap code into mm/zap.c, fork's copying into mm/fork.c -- mirroring
kernel/fork.c, so the mm half of a subsystem sits under the same name.
Large folios are an integral part of mm nowadays and I don't think we
benefit from keeping THP in a separate file.  It is also an opportunity to
shift away from mm/memory.c being a kitchen sink.

David and I talked about this at LSF/MM.  I can give it a try if it fits
your idea of "feature freeze" -- and if it doesn't collide with the series
you have in flight, in which case I'd rather go after yours than around it.

> > Why
> > ===
> >
> > mTHP collapse landed in khugepaged in 7.2 and I was glad to see it.  We
> > at Meta run arm64 with 64K base pages, where a PMD is 512M: PMD-order THP
> > is of limited use at that size, and mTHP is exactly what we want.
> 
> Do you have some numbers that indicate to what degree mTHP khugepaged is
> beneficial?

Not from the fleet yet -- that experiment is still ahead of me, so I can't
give you order-by-order numbers.

What I can say is that on x86 we lean on khugepaged heavily to get THPs in
place; it is not a marginal contributor for us.  On arm64 with 64K base
pages we get nowhere near the x86 numbers without khugepaged being able to
produce mTHP at all.

I'll grant the other half of it, and more strongly than you put it: for a
64K mTHP on a 4K base page the TLB win is modest, and with today's
mechanism -- which clears and flushes the whole 2M PMD to install it -- I
can believe the disruption exceeds the gain and the net effect on a
workload is negative.  That is what I measured: a thread reading and
writing a region while khugepaged collapses it at order-4, read p99 3071ns
against 1023ns.  It shows the disruption is real and that it comes down;
whether the collapse pays for itself at that order is a separate question.

> > khugepaged only ever looks at PMD-aligned windows, and it is not an easy
> > limitation to lift.
> 
> Yes. This assumption is very much baked in.
> 
> I guess this is coming from the perspective of having ranges that are
> neither PMD-aligned nor sized (far harder to achieve with 512 MiB PMD size
> obviously).

Right, and it is the size rather than the alignment that bites.  The real
requirement is that a VMA contain a whole PMD-aligned, PMD-sized range,
which at 2M most anonymous mappings of any size manage and at 512M almost
none do.  That is why the limitation was easy to miss until the PMD got
big.

> > Fixing the alignment is a one-line change, but what it feeds assumes the
> 
> Hmm not so sure about that... especially given how baked in these
> assumptions are.

I think we agree -- that was the setup, not the claim.  Dropping the
ALIGN() is the one line; the point of the sentence is that it buys nothing
on its own, because what you then hand a sub-PMD range to still clears the
whole PMD and still demands the VMA span it.

> Which by the way, all speaks to the need for rework.
> 
> The first stage in my view would be to improve the code to the point that
> these kinds of assumptions fall out of it, which then lays the foundations
> for future changes to eliminate the assumptions.

For the plumbing, yes -- policy, file layout, the scan/run split all
improve by refactoring in place.

I don't think the locking model gets there that way, though, which is why
I built a second engine rather than morphing the first.  The old safety
argument is "hold the address space still"; the new one is "make the
sources inert".  They are not two points on a line -- mmap_write cannot go
before something else holds the sources still, and doing that inside
collapse_huge_page() means replacing the copy, the install and the rollback
at the same time, which is the whole function.  Every halfway state has
neither argument in full.

What is gradual here is the review rather than the mechanism: the engine
arrives one pass at a time, each reviewable alone, with the old one live
until one patch switches over.

> > PMD everywhere that matters: collapse_huge_page() clears and flushes the
> > whole PMD whatever order it is collapsing, installs a PMD leaf because
> > that is the only thing it can produce, and keeps everyone out with
> > mmap_write_lock, anon_vma_lock_write() and an IPI broadcast while it
> > does.
> 
> To be clear - the anon path. I think important to clarify :)

Yes, anon only.  The file path moves into collapse.c and picks up the
scan/run split, but its mechanism is untouched.

And you are right that "installs a PMD leaf" is wrong above: only a
PMD-order collapse installs one, a sub-PMD collapse repopulates the table
with PTEs.  What is order-blind is everything around it -- the PMD is
still cleared and flushed first.

I would like to bring it into the engine as well, and with it the private
copies in MAP_PRIVATE file mappings, which neither path collapses today --
the anon side requires vma_is_anonymous() and the file side works on the
page cache.

I stopped because I wanted to keep the patch count in double digits. :P

> And yeah it does IPI for any sensible arch (with
> CONFIG_MMU_GATHER_RCU_TABLE_FREE) via tlb_remove_table_sync_one(). The
> other arches IPI anyway on TLB invalidation.
> 
> [Though I intend to make all page table freeing RCU relatively soon which
> should? Eliminate the need for this, possibly?]

That would suit this well, and it is worth covering deposited page tables
in it if they are not already in scope.  Today PMD collapse has to deposit
a freshly allocated table rather than redepositing the one it detached,
because a deposited table must be safe for zap_deposited_table() to free
immediately.  Make that free RCU-deferred and the detached table can go
straight back -- one allocation less per PMD collapse.

> However we have to remember that a lot of the user-visible API assumes PMD
> sizing and so the code has to clearly reflect this and make it clear that

Your sentence got cut off, but if this is about the tunables then let me
flag what the series does with them.  max_ptes_none, _swap and _shared are
counts out of a PMD, and a range smaller than one has fewer PTEs than the
budget, so a raw comparison can never refuse it -- a 64K range on 4K pages
is 16 PTEs against a max_ptes_shared default of 256.  For swap and shared
the engine therefore compares fractions: count * HPAGE_PMD_NR against
max * nr_scanned.

max_ptes_none stays as mTHP collapse has it, all-or-nothing: 0, or
everything at that order.  That is deliberate -- allowing holes at an order
below the largest enabled one lets khugepaged fill them and collapse the
result at the next order up, which is the ratchet max_ptes_none exists to
bound.  There is room to scale it at the terminal order, where there is no
larger order to creep into, but I have not done that here.

> > Design
> > ======
> >
> > The old mechanism holds the address space still because it has nothing
> > else stopping the sources from moving under the copy.  The new engine
> > makes the sources themselves inert instead, with the two barriers
> > migration already uses, raised in that order:
> >
> >   1. migration entries replace the source PTEs.  Faults and GUP-slow
> >      now wait on the source folio's lock, which is taken before the
> >      first entry becomes visible.
> >   2. the source folio's refcount is frozen to its expected value.
> >      GUP-fast, pfn walkers, reclaim, compaction and memory-failure all
> >      fail folio_try_get() and back off.
> >
> > Between the two, nothing can reach a source, so the copy runs with no
> > lock held at all -- and the address space is left alone while it does.
> 
> Hmm, are migration entries the right mechnanism here? Are you actually
> migrating the pages to a large folio here, or using them to get the
> behaviour you want on fault/GUP?

Both, and I would argue the behaviour is not a side effect: what a
migration entry means to a waiter -- this page is going away, sleep on its
folio lock and look again -- is exactly true of a source under collapse.
Fault, GUP-slow and rmap then all do the right thing with no new code,
which is the case for reusing the entry rather than inventing a marker
every waiter would have to learn.

What is not reused is mm/migrate.c.  A migration entry encodes one PFN, so
it cannot name an N:1 destination of a different order; the engine takes
the hold-still half and does the remap itself at install.  It is a
migration in substance -- contents move to another folio, the old mappings
are replaced -- but not one migrate.c could drive.

> Same question in general for the freezing.

folio_ref_freeze() means nobody may take a new reference, which is the
property the copy needs, and is why migration and split use it too.

> > What that removes from every collapse path:
> >
> >   mmap_write_lock              -> mmap_read
> >   anon_vma_lock_write()        -> nothing: an rmap walk needs the folio
> >                                   locked, and the engine holds that lock
> >                                   from freeze to putback
> 
> I do like the idea of eliminating uses of the rmap lock like this, not only
> for contention's sake but also for scalable CoW purposes which introduces
> challenges with regards to holding these.
> 
> In fact, migration and huge memory collapse are the really problematic
> areas.

If that is about their rmap complexity, collapse gets easier here rather
than harder.

The engine takes no rmap lock and walks no rmap.  A page shared with
another process is unshared before anything is frozen -- the fault-in
pass breaks CoW, exactly as a write would -- so by freeze time a source
is exclusive to this mm and its only live mappings are the ones being
replaced.  Migration has to cope with a folio mapped from many mms; this
never sees one.

If what scalable CoW needs is that collapse stops messing with rmap,
that is what this does.

> 
> >   tlb_remove_table_sync_one()  -> nothing: one ranged flush per round
> 
> Aren't we reliant upon this synchronisation for correctness?

Not in the new engine.

In collapse_huge_page() the IPI is what makes the *detached* table safe
to use: it pmdp_collapse_flush()es the PMD and then copies out of the
table it just detached, so it has to know no lockless walker is still
inside it.

The new engine never does that -- a sub-PMD window is collapsed in place
under the page table lock, so nothing is detached, and at PMD order the
table is detached, never touched again, and freed with pte_free_defer().
The synchronisation is still there, it is RCU rather than an IPI; and on
the arches without RCU table free the flush itself IPIs, as you say.

> >  - A table that cannot become one huge page still yields the largest
> >    windows inside it, where before a single disqualified PTE gave up
> >    the whole table.
> 
> Are you permitting collapse of ranges that straddle PTEs?

No -- a candidate never crosses a page table or a VMA.  A round works
within one table, and each candidate is validated against the VMA at its
own order.

> Though in general I'm confused by the single disqualified PTE here -

Taking that literally is how I meant it: collapse_scan_pmd() goto

clean lazyfree, off the LRU, unexpected refcount -- and mthp_collapse() only
runs if the verdict came back SCAN_SUCCEED.  So one
such PTE anywhere in the table means nothing in that table collapses, at
any order, even at an order whose windows avoid it entirely.

> > There may be a way out -- a PMD migration entry over the table during
> > the window, so the CPU never caches a walk to shoot down -- but that
> > means teaching every pmd-level walker a new kind of entry, and I have
> > not tried it.
>

I find it rather elegant, and expect it to be minimally intrusive: let such
a PMD be walkable exactly as a present one is, so software descends through
it as usual while the CPU sees a non-present entry and caches nothing.
Transparent to software, opaque to the CPU.

Out of scope for this patchset either way.

--

review_comments.author: Kiryl Shutsemau (author)
review_comments.summary: Author addressed concerns about the patch series' complexity and maintainability, explaining that it's not a cleanup but a replacement of an existing mechanism. He acknowledged that the current locking is 'nasty', but argued that the new engine changes the serialization model in a way that improves scalability. The author proposed to incrementally improve the code by adding the new engine alongside the old one and then removing the old mechanism, rather than trying to refactor everything at once.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, Aug 18, 2026 at 04:12:17PM +0200, David Hildenbrand (Arm) wrote:
> I think we all agree that there is a lot of room for improvement, but the big
> question is:
> 
> (a) When does it stop being a cleanup and is a new feature in disguise that
>     makes the code more complicated and even harder to maintain.
> 
> (b) Can it just naturally be made looking like a cleanup.
> 
> Ideally, we'd get b), in small, nice-to-review chunks that incrementally improve
> the code without inflating it heavily or moving everything around.

It is not a cleanup and I would rather not sell it as one.  It replaces a
mechanism, so judged as (b) it fails by construction.

I believe the end result is much cleaner. But I might be biased. :)

> The current locking is nasty, so anything that moves us one step closer into
> something that is not only simpler but also more scalable is nice. I am a bit
> concerned with the churn in the series as is.
> 
> After this series, mm/collapse.c itself is way larger than just mm/khugepaged.c
> originally, which raises some eyebrows.

Line count is a poor proxy for simplicity or scalability.  What the
engine changes is the serialization model, and that is the part collapse
needs changed: the PMD granularity and the exclusion both come out of
the locking.

Incremental does not reach it, though.  The old mechanism is correct
because it holds mmap_write_lock, the anon_vma write lock and a reference
from the LRU; the engine is correct because the sources are frozen behind
migration entries.  There is no halfway state that is correct under both,
so the switch lands as one patch.

What can be incremental is everything around it: the engine goes in beside
the old mechanism, patch 25 points the anon path at it, and 28 removes what
it replaces.  Until 28 both are in the tree with only one of them
reachable, so the switch can be reverted on its own.

> We should also be aware that people are proposing file/shmem mTHP collapse, so
> ideally what we refactor would naturally unify some of these code paths.
> 
> I am wondering whether shmem mTHP collapse should come first. (I'm hoping that
> shmem mTHP collapse can unify some of the anon+file collapse code in a nice way,
> to similarly just look like a cleanup while enabling a new scenario.

mTHP collapse as it stands has limited usability: PMD-aligned windows only,
and one VMA has to own the PMD.  Bolting file collapse onto the same
structure adds to the debt instead of paying it down.

It would fit the new design.  The frame -- scan, candidate selection, the
round and its passes -- has nothing anon-specific in it; what is
anon-specific sits in the freeze (folio_test_anon(), PageAnonExclusive())
and the unshare in the fault-in pass.  A file source would bring its own
check, freeze, copy and install.

I am not sure it should, though.

Do we want to find file collapse candidates by walking the virtual
address space at all?

collapse_file() already works on the mapping -- it builds the folio in
the page cache and then repairs every mapping through
retract_page_tables() -- so the VMA walk only picks which inode range to
try, and it reaches only what a registered mm maps right now.  Large
folios buy more than TLB reach: fewer page cache entries, cheaper
writeback, natural locking batch, etc.  Those apply whether the file is
mapped or not, and going at the inode directly would reach them.

> Agreed, I think we really should unify+cleanup the existing code first before
> doing more drastic changes.
> 
> Having a series that throws all of khugepaged.c into a mixer and pours something
> new into collapse.c is ... concerning :)

The moving around is patches 29-35 and the tracing after them.  None of it
is needed for the engine: 1-28 add it, switch the anon path over and delete
the old mechanism, without moving anything else out of khugepaged.c.  If
the churn is the problem, v2 can stop there and the moves can come later as
their own series.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

---

On Tue, Aug 18, 2026 at 04:15:27PM +0200, David Hildenbrand (Arm) wrote:
> > David and I talked about this at LSF/MM. 
> 
> Ah, I missed the context in my other reply. Lorenzo already had some patches at
> some point to split up mm/memory.c into better chunks that will also better help
> our subcomponent maintenance model.

Lorenzo, if you can dig those out, I would rather build on them than start
over.  Happy to do the legwork.

> I think the challenge is how to handle huge_memory.c, because ideally, we'd not
> have these stupid callbacks into huge_memory.c once we make PMDs just a
> first-class citizen.

Agreed on settling the target shape before moving anything.

Splitting by operation answers most of huge_memory.c on its own, though.

Its entry points are named after the operation they implement, and each has
one destination: do_huge_pmd_anonymous_page(), do_huge_pmd_wp_page() and
do_huge_pmd_numa_page() belong next to do_anonymous_page() in
mm/fault.c.

zap_huge_pmd() next to zap_pte_range(), copy_huge_pmd() next to

have their callers in the right file already -- mprotect.c, mremap.c, gup.c
-- so they move to the caller.  The callback goes away because the PMD case
becomes a branch beside the PTE case instead of a call into another file.

-- 
  Kiryl Shutsemau / Kirill A. Shutemov

> > Ah, I missed the context in my other reply. Lorenzo already had some patches at

Oh, well, I can give it a try from scratch.

review_comments.raw_body:
On Sun Aug 16, 2026 at 6:45 PM EDT, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>
>
> Yes, I know, this is a lot of changes. But I'm happy with the overall state
> of the patchset and the only reason I tag it as RFC is that it is tricky
> to get 57 patches upstream.
>
> I wanted to give a view of the end state first. I will suggest a possible
> way to split it below.
>
> I would appreciate any feedback.
>
> TL;DR
> =====
>
> This replaces khugepaged's anonymous collapse with an engine that
> can collapse sub-PMD ranges. It is built around migration entries and
> frozen folios instead of heavy locking and isolation, aiming for better
> scalability and less disruption to the workload being collapsed.
>
> Why
> ===
>
> mTHP collapse landed in khugepaged in 7.2 and I was glad to see it.  We
> at Meta run arm64 with 64K base pages, where a PMD is 512M: PMD-order THP
> is of limited use at that size, and mTHP is exactly what we want.
>
> It turned out not to help us.
>
> khugepaged only ever looks at PMD-aligned windows, and it is not an easy
> limitation to lift.
>
> Fixing the alignment is a one-line change, but what it feeds assumes the
> PMD everywhere that matters: collapse_huge_page() clears and flushes the
> whole PMD whatever order it is collapsing, installs a PMD leaf because
> that is the only thing it can produce, and keeps everyone out with
> mmap_write_lock, anon_vma_lock_write() and an IPI broadcast while it
> does.
>
> Which is why hugepage_vma_revalidate() demands that the VMA span the
> whole PMD even for an mTHP order -- "we'd need to lock all VMAs in the
> PMD range to support this", as the comment there puts it.  A PMD-granular
> operation is only safe when one VMA owns the PMD, and that is exactly the
> restriction in the way.  The alignment is the symptom; the PMD is the
> design.
>
> So both roots have to go.

I agree that khugepaged is designed for PMD-aligned collapse and this is
a limitation we want to get rid of. It is great you are looking at them.

>
> Design
> ======
>
> The old mechanism holds the address space still because it has nothing
> else stopping the sources from moving under the copy.  The new engine
> makes the sources themselves inert instead, with the two barriers
> migration already uses, raised in that order:
>
>   1. migration entries replace the source PTEs.  Faults and GUP-slow
>      now wait on the source folio's lock, which is taken before the
>      first entry becomes visible.
>   2. the source folio's refcount is frozen to its expected value.
>      GUP-fast, pfn walkers, reclaim, compaction and memory-failure all
>      fail folio_try_get() and back off.
>
> Between the two, nothing can reach a source, so the copy runs with no
> lock held at all -- and the address space is left alone while it does.
>
> What that removes from every collapse path:
>
>   mmap_write_lock              -> mmap_read
>   anon_vma_lock_write()        -> nothing: an rmap walk needs the folio
>                                   locked, and the engine holds that lock
>                                   from freeze to putback
>   tlb_remove_table_sync_one()  -> nothing: one ranged flush per round
>   LRU isolation                -> nothing: sources are inert in place

I remember we were discussing using migration entry and the issue with
mmap_write_lock() in the context of in-place THP promotion and the
conclusion was that because MADV_DONTNEED (maybe MADV_REMOVE or
MADV_PAGEOUT) works on page table and does not change VMAs,
mmap_write_lock() is needed to prevent things being changed under
khugepaged. Anything different in normal khugepaged collapse process, so
that it is OK to use mmap_read_lock? Let me know if I misremember it.

Thanks.

-- 
Best Regards,
Yan, Zi
