>          that does anything: stop earlier and the tree carries an
>          engine nothing calls
>   28     remove the mechanism the engine replaces
>   29-42  moving what is left of collapse out of khugepaged.c, and the
>          engine's own tracepoints
>   43-49  per-VMA locking
>   50-57  selftests and MAINTAINERS
>
> Keeping the removal separate leaves both engines in the tree with only
> the new one reachable, so the switch can be reverted on its own if
> something turns up.  The old mechanism is already carried that way for
> three patches inside the series, so this costs nothing but 975 lines of
> unreferenced code until 28 lands.  That safety net only lasts until the
> blocks after it land, though: once collapse has moved out of
> khugepaged.c and the locking has changed, reverting the switch no longer
> gives back a working old engine.

Again as above, no to these changes in any form at the moment.

The techical debt must be paid down first.

>
> Base and dependencies
> =====================
>
> This applies on the selftests series, not on plain mm-new:
>
>   [PATCH v4 00/19] selftests/mm: improve khugepaged coverage
>   https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260815015901.1236937-1-kirill@shutemov.name/
>
> which is on mm-new 33f61b12d297.
>
> Patches 43-49 depend on Suren's unconditional per-VMA locks:
>
>   [PATCH v6 0/5] mm: Unconditional per-VMA locks and cleanups
>   https://lore.kernel.org/all/20260813193433.3318288-1-surenb@google.com/
>
> That series is not in mm-new yet, and with patch 46 applied SMP=n does
> not build without it: lock_next_vma() is behind CONFIG_PER_VMA_LOCK in
> mmap_lock.h.  Everything up to patch 42 builds and runs on mm-new as it
> stands.  There is no fallback path by choice -- adding one would mean
> carrying two locking models through every pass.
>
> Both branches are available at
>
>   git://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/kas/linux.git collapse/rfc-v1
>
> and the benchmark used for the numbers below, which is unposted and not a
> dependency, at
>
>   git://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/kas/linux.git perf/bench-usemem

As above.

>
> Performance
> ===========
>
> Measuring khugepaged is awkward.  It is a background daemon, so what
> matters is what a workload feels while it runs, not what the daemon
> reports about itself -- and the usual coverage instrument is no help
> below the PMD: smaps AnonHugePages only counts PMD-order folios, so it
> reads zero however much mTHP has been collapsed.
>
> So I wrote "perf bench mem usemem" for this.  It touches a region while
> khugepaged works on it and reports the workload's own latency
> percentiles and throughput, against per-size counters that can see
> sub-PMD folios.  The branch is above; it is unposted and not a
> dependency.
>
> x86-64, production configs (no KASAN, no lockdep, no DEBUG_VM, no
> PAGE_TABLE_CHECK), interleaved rounds on an idle host, equal work on
> every arm.
>
> I measured three kernels, so the two halves of the series can be told
> apart in the numbers below:
>
>   A   the base
>   B   the new engine, still under mmap_read
>   C   B plus per-VMA locking -- what this series ends up with
>
> The engine: a sub-PMD collapse stops blanking the surrounding 2M
> -----------------------------------------------------------------
>
> base routes sub-PMD collapse through collapse_huge_page(), whose
> pmdp_collapse_flush() and tlb_remove_table_sync_one() are not gated on
> order: to collapse an order-4 window of 16 pages it clears and flushes
> the whole 512-page PMD and IPIs, then repopulates.  The engine does the
> window under the PTL.
>
> A thread reading and writing a 32G region while it is collapsed at
> order-4, 16384 collapses on every arm:
>
>                          A        B        C
>   read p99 (ns)       3071     1023     1023   -66.7%
>   write p99 (ns)      3071      927      927   -69.8%
>
> and the workload's read rate rises by 68% on both engine kernels.
>
> B == C, so this is the engine, not the locking.
>
> At PMD order the same workload is flat, and that is expected rather
> than disappointing: it is the one configuration where both mechanisms
> disturb exactly the same 2M.  Read it as no regression at PMD order.
>
> Per-VMA locking: address-space operations stop waiting on the scan
> -------------------------------------------------------------------
>
> MADV_HUGEPAGE/MADV_NOHUGEPAGE toggling against a scanning mm, which is
> what jemalloc does with its arenas.  4096 collapses on every arm:
>
>                          A        B        C
>   ops/sec           340656   340820   603305   +77%
>   p99 (ns)           77823    86015     3327   -96%
>   p99.9 (ns)         86015    94207     9215   -89%
>
> B is about 11% worse than base at p99 here, consistently across runs:
> the engine alone slightly worsens hint-toggle latency, and per-VMA
> locking is what turns it into a win.  Both halves are in this series, so
> C is what a reviewer gets, but the middle column is the honest one.
>
> The trade is real in the other direction too.  On settled memory with
> nothing to collapse and scan_sleep_millisecs=0, per-VMA locking costs
> about 47% of scan throughput against one mmap_read for the whole walk.
> That is a synthetic worst case -- the daemon wraps 8000 times a second
> there, where production defaults to 10s between passes -- and it buys
> mmap/munmap p99 of 56us against 1.4us.
>
> Collapse itself is not slower
> -----------------------------
>
> One complete pass over a 32G region, 16384 collapses, khugepaged CPU
> from /proc/<pid>/stat, 7 repeats:
>
>   A base    median 5760 ms   spread 12.7%
>   B engine  median 4990 ms   spread  3.8%
>   C pervma  median 5020 ms   spread 12.4%
>
> The base arm is bimodal, so its median moves with sampling and the
> percentage is soft.  The distribution-free statement is better: every
> engine run used less CPU than every base run.
>
> The engine also allocates one destination per folio installed, where
> base allocates 5.25 and frees the rest again: nothing is allocated until
> the sources are frozen and the collapse can no longer be refused.
>
> A measurement note, since an earlier version of this series quoted worse
> figures.  khugepaged CPU has to be measured per collapse or per
> completed pass, never over a fixed window with scan_sleep_millisecs=0:
> the daemon never sleeps, so whichever kernel finishes the work sooner
> spends the rest of the window scanning settled memory and is charged for
> it.  Measured that way the engine appeared to cost 10% more CPU;
> measured per unit of work it costs less.
>
> Costs
> =====
>
> At PMD order the engine issues two TLB flushes per collapse where the
> old mechanism issues one: the freeze's ranged flush plus the terminal
> layer's pmdp_collapse_flush().  A PMD candidate is alone in its round,
> so nothing amortizes the first.  Dropping the old per-collapse
> tlb_remove_table_sync_one() IPI presumably pays for it, but that was not
> measured and is not claimed here.
>
> There may be a way out -- a PMD migration entry over the table during
> the window, so the CPU never caches a walk to shoot down -- but that
> means teaching every pmd-level walker a new kind of entry, and I have
> not tried it.

Hmm this seems like complexity on top of complexity...

>
> PMD collapse deposits a freshly allocated page table instead of
> redepositing the detached one.  Whoever withdraws a deposited table
> frees it immediately, with nothing to hold a lockless walker off first,
> and under a read lock the detached table may still be traversed by
> GUP-fast or an RCU pte walk.  It goes to pte_free_defer() instead,
> exactly as retract_page_tables() does.  One transient table page per PMD
> collapse buys the IPI's absence.
>
> That cost goes away if zap_deposited_table() -- the only site that frees
> a deposited table outright, the others redeposit it or repopulate the
> PMD with it -- used pte_free_defer().  The deposit would no longer have
> to be quiescent and the detached table could go straight back.  It would
> defer every THP zap's table free, and I have not tried it.
>
> A shared source now costs an extra copy.  The freeze needs every page
> exclusive to this mm, so the fault-in pass breaks CoW first -- an
> allocation and a copy -- and the collapse then copies that page into the
> destination; the old mechanism copied a shared page straight into the
> new folio and broke the sharing that way.  It is bounded by
> max_ptes_shared, which khugepaged holds at zero below the PMD order, so
> in practice this is PMD-order collapse and MADV_COLLAPSE.

Hmm I guess better to be explicit.

>
> Size
> ====
>
> mm/ grows by 1915 lines net: 4475 added against 2560 deleted.
>
> That is not a claim that this is less code, but it is less than it
> looks.  khugepaged.c goes from 3283 lines to 908.  The new engine is
> 4052 lines across mm/collapse.c and mm/collapse.h, of which 1344 --
> about a third -- are comments, which is where the pipeline's invariants
> are written down.  What replaces three install paths with their own
> isolate/copy/rollback is one engine and one contract.

As above. The existing codebase is a mess and must be cleaned up first,
this isn't optional.

>
> Testing
> =======
>
> Both matrices run the mm selftests plus a race harness, on the
> validation config: KASAN, lockdep, PROVE_LOCKING, DEBUG_VM and
> PAGE_TABLE_CHECK, 16G of guest memory, swap active so the swap-in
> prepass is exercised rather than skipped.
>
>   x86-64        433 pass, 0 fail, 12 skip
>   arm64/64K     581 pass, 0 fail, 18 skip
>
> dmesg clean on both.  The arm64 skips are a pre-existing shmem
> MADV_COLLAPSE -EINVAL on 64K pages, confirmed against the base by A/B.
>
> Every one of the 57 patches builds with no new warnings; !NUMA and !MMU
> (arm nommu) build clean.  SMP=n does not build, for the reason in the

>
> The race harness also gets longer soaks -- 1800s per driver mode, with

On Mon, Aug 17, 2026 at 02:38:44PM +0100, Kiryl Shutsemau wrote:
> David and I talked about this at LSF/MM.  I can give it a try if it fits

Whether intended or not you sound rather like you are trying to override me
in favour of my co-maintainer here and it's... not helpful.

David and I co-maintain THP together, are in constant communication, and
have a great working relationship :)

IOW - if one of us states a position on the sub(sub?)system - then take
that to be the actual position.

I have poured what must be hundreds of hours now into THP maintainership -
it's by far my biggest workload on the maintenance front, by far the most
painful and by far the most thankless.

I do it because I care about mm a great deal and am, frankly, driven by a
desire to see THP turn from a flaming trash pile of a code base with
confusing semantics and many, many broken parts into something that serves
the community's needs with far less maintenance burden.

Looking over your series it seems some of the patches works in this
direction (great!), but much else of it fundamentally changes key
behaviour.

So it's just a question of deferring the latter until we get to a sane
point with the former.

I keep talking about this stuff because companies are motivated by wanting
to solve their problems (understandably) but if nobody pushes back then THP
will continue to be a series of changes lumped on top of one another adding
more and more technical debt.

--

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the Btrfs file system where, on transaction commit failure, the tree log mutex is released before aborting the transaction. This allows a subsequent log sync to write superblocks that point to tree blocks not yet written to disk, causing a parent transid mismatch on next mount. The patch restores the correct ordering by aborting the transaction while still holding the tree log mutex, which records the fs error and prevents the superblock from being written.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 01/11] mm, swap: add virtual swap device infrastructure
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces the virtual swap device infrastructure, which allows for dynamic allocation of swap space and enables features like zswap and zero-filled pages without a physical swap device. The virtual swap device is created when the 'vswap' kernel parameter is set to 'on', and it lives for the lifetime of the kernel. The patch also includes changes to various files such as mm/swap.h, mm/page_io.c, and mm/vswap.h to support this new infrastructure. The dynamic-cluster allocator is wired in, but no allocation path can select it yet, with subsequent patches expected to add the necessary paths.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/11] mm, swap: support zswap and zero-filled swap pages as vswap backends
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for zswap and zero-filled swap pages as virtual swap (vswap) backends, allowing compressed or zero-filled pages to be stored without pre-allocating physical swap slots. The vswap layer decouples PTE swap entries from physical backing, enabling efficient compression and detection of zero-filled pages. However, this patch only supports zswap and zero-page backends, with physical disk backing and real writeback to be implemented in later patches. Additionally, THP (Transparent Huge Pages) swapin is disabled for vswap entries until further development.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 03/11] mm, swap: prepare the swap IO path for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the Linux kernel's swap IO path to support virtual swap (vswap) by allowing it to submit IO for a swap entry other than folio->swap. The current implementation derives the target device and sector from folio->swap, which is not suitable for vswap entries backed by physical slots. To address this, the patch introduces a new field in the swap_iocb structure to store the sector of the swap entry, and updates various functions to use this new field instead of folio->swap. This change enables the batching path to serve both vswap entries and physical entries mapped directly into PTEs without any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 04/11] mm, swap: support physical swap as a vswap backend
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for physical swap as a backend for the virtual swap layer, allowing zswap to decline pages and allocate physical slots on demand. The physical slot is tracked via a pointer-tagged swap_table entry, and readahead scans are modified to skip these entries. The patch also includes changes to handle failed reads of vswap entries and to bypass vswap when zswap is disabled at the host level or for the folio's cgroup.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 05/11] mm, swap: enable THP swapin for vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch enables the swapping in of large anonymous memory pages (THP) for vswap entries when they share a contiguous run of physical swap slots on a synchronous IO device. This allows for more efficient swapping and reduces the number of faults that occur during the process. The patch also introduces checks to ensure that zswap-backed or mixed-backing batches are not swapped in as THPs, and that fault retries occur at smaller orders when necessary.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 06/11] mm, swap: write back vswap zswap entries to physical swap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds support for writing back zswap-backed vswap entries to physical swap. It mirrors the existing zswap writeback path, but allocates physical backing on demand at writeback time instead of pre-allocating it. The zswap shrinker no longer skips vswap entries unless there is not enough physical swap space available. This allows for more efficient use of swap space and improves system performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 07/11] mm, swap: reclaim physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch reclaims physical slots backing cache-only vswap entries when the swap is more than half used. Cache-only vswap entries are those where the vswap entry's swap_count has dropped to 0, but its folio is still in the swap cache. The patch introduces a new flag, SWP_RMAP_CACHE_ONLY, to mark such entries and allows reclaiming their physical slots from the physical reclaim scanner. This change aims to free up physical capacity for new allocations when the swap usage exceeds half of the available space.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 08/11] mm, swap: only charge physical swap entries
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the way memory swap is charged to a cgroup's memcg->swap counter. Instead of charging when a vswap entry is allocated, it charges only when the entry acquires physical backing. This change ensures that zswap-backed and zero-filled pages are not counted towards the cgroup's swap usage. The patch also refactors the swap memcg operations into separate helpers for getting, recording, charging, uncharging, and putting the owner, which is a prerequisite for this change. As a result, memory.swap.current will only count on-disk swap usage, allowing cgroups to reclaim their anon memory even with memory.swap.max set to 0 if zswap is enabled.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 09/11] mm, swap: add debugfs counters for vswap
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two debugfs counters to track virtual swap usage in the Linux kernel. The first counter, 'used', tracks the number of virtual swap slots (pages) currently allocated. The second counter, 'alloc_reject', counts the cumulative number of pages that failed to get a vswap slot. These counters are exposed under the '/sys/kernel/debug/vswap/' directory and provide visibility into virtual swap allocation behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 10/11] mm, swap: defer memcg_table allocation for physical swap clusters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory allocation for swap clusters by deferring the allocation of a memcg table until it's actually needed. This is done to reduce unnecessary memory usage in cases where a physical swap cluster only holds vswap backings, which don't require a memcg table. The patch allocates the table eagerly for vswap clusters and for physical clusters when vswap is disabled or not enabled. Otherwise, allocation is deferred until the first direct-use slot is handed out.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 11/11] mm, swap: widen swap_info_struct max/pages to unsigned long
series_items.patch_summary: This patch widens the size of swap_info_struct's max and pages fields from unsigned int to unsigned long, allowing the vswap device to exceed its previous 16 TB capacity limit when using 4 KB pages. The new maximum capacity is determined by the cluster_info_pool xarray's allocator limit, which can store up to ~8 PB at a typical SWAPFILE_CLUSTER=512 layout. This change enables larger swap devices and improves system performance for systems with high memory demands.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces Virtual Swap Space (VSwap), a new swap space management system that allows for efficient allocation and deallocation of swap slots. VSwap is designed to handle the complexities of modern swap optimizations, such as zswap-backed and zero-filled pages. The patches refactor the swap memcg operations into separate get, record, charge, uncharge, and put helpers, and introduce debugfs counters for vswap usage and allocation rejection.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 1/8] mm/gup: break out gup_fill_pages() helper
series_items.patch_summary: This patch breaks out a helper function called gup_fill_pages() from the __get_user_pages() function in mm/gup.c. series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 2/8] mm/gup: convert follow_page_mask() to return a long
series_items.patch_summary: This patch changes the return type of follow_page_mask() and its helper functions from struct page pointer to long. The function now returns 0, a negative errno, or 1 with the page stored in a new pages[0] slot. This allows the return value to carry a page count rather than a single struct page pointer.

review_comments.author: John Hubbard
review_comments.summary:
reviewer noted that marking a page dirty in follow_page_pte_commit() can lead to issues with file system coordination, and suggested this as another problem beyond the initial concern about splitting the function

Reviewer John Hubbard pointed out a technical issue where marking a file-backed page dirty is not allowed after other preparation steps have been run, citing ext4's documentation and its own workaround using folio_set_checked(). He noted that the current implementation of unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock() is also in an awkward state.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yes, I agree about that problem, but it's not the only one. It turns
out that the only thing worse than failing to mark a page dirty is
marking it dirty without coordinating with the filesystem.

---

Well...on a file-backed page, marking it dirty is the *last* step of
a sequence, and a driver cannot run the earlier steps.

ext4_page_mkwrite() into ext4_block_page_mkwrite() runs it in this
order:

	sb_start_pagefault(inode->i_sb);	/* freeze protection */
	file_update_time(vma->vm_file);
	filemap_invalidate_lock_shared(mapping);	/* truncate */
	ext4_journal_start(inode, EXT4_HT_WRITE_PAGE, credits);
	ext4_block_write_begin(handle, folio, 0, len, get_block);
	folio_mark_dirty(folio);
	ext4_journal_stop(handle);
	folio_wait_stable(folio);

A set_page_dirty() at the driver's write site is that
folio_mark_dirty(), but with none of the preparation above it.

ext4 documents this case already, in ext4_journalled_dirty_folio() on
the data=journal path:

  * ... except for the case when someone
  * had the page pinned and dirtied the page through this pin (e.g. by doing
  * direct IO to it). In that case we'd need to attach buffers here to the
  * transaction but we cannot due to lock ordering.

Its workaround is folio_set_checked(), which defers the real work to
ext4_writepages(). If ext4 can't do the preparation from inside the
dirty call, a driver can't either.

So for a file-backed page there's nothing the driver can add. What's
missing is a way for the filesystem to be told before the device
writes, and to revoke the pin when it needs to, which is where the
lease proposals come in. None of that exists today.

And yes, unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock() is in the same awkward mess.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

This improves performance by eliminating redundant work for adjacent pages from different folios or plain base pages with no folio relationship. series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH v3 8/8] mm/gup: batch contiguous same-folio PTEs into one refcount grab

review_comments.author: John Hubbard
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that marking a page dirty in follow_page_mask() can lead to issues if not coordinated with the filesystem, and agreed that this is one of several problems

Reviewer noted that ext4_page_mkwrite() and other drivers cannot run set_page_dirty() on a file-backed page because it requires preparation steps like sb_start_pagefault(), file_update_time(), and filemap_invalidate_lock_shared() to be executed before folio_mark_dirty(). The reviewer suggested that the filesystem needs a way to be told before the device writes, which is where lease proposals come in.
review_comments.raw_body:
Yes, I agree about that problem, but it's not the only one. It turns
out that the only thing worse than failing to mark a page dirty is
marking it dirty without coordinating with the filesystem.

---

Well...on a file-backed page, marking it dirty is the *last* step of
a sequence, and a driver cannot run the earlier steps.

ext4_page_mkwrite() into ext4_block_page_mkwrite() runs it in this
order:

	sb_start_pagefault(inode->i_sb);	/* freeze protection */
	file_update_time(vma->vm_file);
	filemap_invalidate_lock_shared(mapping);	/* truncate */
	ext4_journal_start(inode, EXT4_HT_WRITE_PAGE, credits);
	ext4_block_write_begin(handle, folio, 0, len, get_block);
	folio_mark_dirty(folio);
	ext4_journal_stop(handle);
	folio_wait_stable(folio);

A set_page_dirty() at the driver's write site is that
folio_mark_dirty(), but with none of the preparation above it.

ext4 documents this case already, in ext4_journalled_dirty_folio() on
the data=journal path:

  * ... except for the case when someone
  * had the page pinned and dirtied the page through this pin (e.g. by doing
  * direct IO to it). In that case we'd need to attach buffers here to the
  * transaction but we cannot due to lock ordering.

Its workaround is folio_set_checked(), which defers the real work to
ext4_writepages(). If ext4 can't do the preparation from inside the
dirty call, a driver can't either.

So for a file-backed page there's nothing the driver can add. What's
missing is a way for the filesystem to be told before the device
writes, and to revoke the pin when it needs to, which is where the
lease proposals come in. None of that exists today.

And yes, unpin_user_pages_dirty_lock() is in the same awkward mess.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/4] kernfs: Use VFS lookup context in d_revalidate()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the kernfs revalidation callback to use VFS-provided lookup context instead of recovering information from mutable dentry fields. The patch also prepares the callback for lockless operation by comparing names using their explicit length, which may point into the pathname and need not be terminated at name->len. This change is intended to improve stability and performance in concurrent rename scenarios.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/4] kernfs: Prepare directory revisions for lockless reads
series_items.patch_summary: This patch prepares the directory revisions in the Linux kernel's kernfs subsystem for lockless reads by annotating accesses to parent directory generations and revision updates with READ_ONCE() and WRITE_ONCE(). This allows the comparison of directory revisions to safely move outside the kernfs_rwsem semaphore, improving performance. The writer contract in kernfs_inc_rev() is also asserted to ensure that revision updates remain serialized.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/4] kernfs: Avoid namespace dereference in d_revalidate()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the kernfs module to avoid dereferencing a namespace tag in the d_revalidate() function, which can lead to issues when kernfs_rename_ns() replaces the tag. Instead of comparing namespace IDs, it uses pointer equality for this non-user-visible check. The change is made because kn->ns will become a lockless read in the next commit, and marking both sides of it now ensures that the read and stores are properly synchronized.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/4] kernfs: Remove kernfs_rwsem from dentry revalidation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes the kernfs_rwsem lock from dentry revalidation in the Linux kernel's kernfs subsystem. The lock was previously taken to ensure a coherent snapshot, but it is no longer necessary as the answer returned by ->d_revalidate() is already stale when it returns. The patch replaces the lock with an RCU read lock and uses data_race() to mark reads that are not protected by the lock. This change reduces contention sites in kernfs_dop_revalidate() and improves performance for readers walking cgroupfs and sysfs against concurrent cgroup and netdev churn.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the performance of kernfs by removing the kernfs_rwsem from dentry revalidation. The current implementation causes contention and convoying in reader path-walks, leading to significant slowdowns. The patches propose using VFS lookup context in d_revalidate(), annotating directory revisions for lockless access, avoiding namespace dereferences, and finally removing the kernfs_rwsem. These changes are expected to improve reader path-walk throughput by 35-53%.
